meta.title: Pass or perish: rate-gated selective regimes on the Hadean Earth
meta.subtitle: OR: What a 4.2 Ga LUCA tells us about the tempo of prebiotic selection
meta.notes: Machine-readable extraction of every sheet of the Pass-or-perish figure-data workbook (README, Vocabulary, Method_time_budgets, Fig1 to Fig8, Elements_considered, Pi_ratio, Measurement_gaps, References) plus prose definitions from manuscript_v5.md. Excel formulas in the workbook have been evaluated and stored as numbers. Wording is taken from the workbook and the manuscript wherever it exists. Conventions carried over from the workbook README: all times in seconds unless a field name says otherwise; Myr means million years; ranges are stored as separate low and high fields. Three fields are new to this model and are not in the workbook: scenarios.n_parallel_sites_low, scenarios.n_parallel_sites_high and scenarios.site_note (all Tier C, derived here from the reasoning text), measurement_gaps.linked_prediction (Tier C except for Gap 6, which the sheet itself ties to prediction 2), and references.tier (Tier C, assigned from the figures each source supports). Elements considered but not given a matrix row, with their reasons, are on the Elements_considered sheet of the workbook: tungsten and molybdenum and potassium are discussed in the text only, and cobalt, selenium, boron, zinc and copper are not carried, copper being kept as the control case for prediction 2. The elements array here holds the nine rows of the Figure 3 passage matrix. Verdict and ratio columns of Fig2, the cycle counts of Fig6, the component sums of Fig8 and the geometric mean block of Fig7 are live formulas in the workbook and are recomputed by the app from the stored inputs rather than stored as text.
meta.model_additions: This file extends the manuscript v5 dataset with the preservation rung S6 and its two gates (S6a ecosystem persistence, S6b rock-record preservation), an S6 grade and reason for every element, and per-scenario parallel-site counts. Everything new is tagged Tier C or carries its own tier and sources. S6 sits after S5 and does not consume the pre-LUCA budget: it is a filter on the evidence, not on life.
meta.preservation_note: S6 comes after S5 and does not consume the pre-LUCA budget. It is a filter on the evidence rather than on life. Nothing about S6 had to happen before LUCA existed. But S6 decides what we are allowed to see, so it decides which of the earlier rungs can ever be tested against a rock. Two gates have to be passed in order. First the lineage has to become a community, because LUCA was not alone and a single cell line in a single vessel leaves no measurable trace. Second, some product of that community has to be chemically inert enough, and physically protected enough, to survive four billion years of burial.

tiers.label: Tier A, real numbers
tiers.definition: Real numbers. Lifetimes, rate constants and fluxes of chemical species in water and in the atmosphere, taken from measured kinetics or from published photochemical models. These can be checked against a source.

tiers.label: Tier B, order of magnitude only
tiers.definition: Order of magnitude only. The time needed to assemble a network, to fix a trait in a population, or for a whole scenario family to run. These exist only as ranges and are presented as ranges. They are explicit so that they can be argued with, not because they are precise.

tiers.label: Tier C, derived for this model
tiers.definition: Not a tier used in the manuscript or the workbook. It marks the few values that were derived for this interactive model rather than transcribed from a source: the number of parallel sites per scenario, the prediction each measurement gap is linked to where the sheet does not say, and the tier assigned to each reference. Every Tier C value carries its reasoning in the record itself.

speed_classes.label: Class 1, effectively instantaneous, from microseconds to hours
speed_classes.description: These steps are fast because they are single chemical or physical events, and their rates are either measured or bounded by measurement. The important point about Class 1 is not that these steps are fast. It is that they are the steps the handoff criterion says are most at risk, and they are fast enough to beat destruction whenever the geometry is right.

speed_classes.label: Class 2, fast on human timescales, from days to thousands of years
speed_classes.description: These are the accumulation steps, and they are slower than Class 1 because they depend on transport rather than on chemistry.

speed_classes.label: Class 3, genuinely slow, from a million years upwards
speed_classes.description: Only two things in the sequence appear to require geological time, and both sit at the top of the ladder: crossing the error threshold and establishing heritability, which is the S4 to S5 chokepoint, and fixing a trait or an enzyme family in a population, for which the standard working estimates land at 10^6 to 10^7 years.

rungs.name: availability and delivery
rungs.mechanism: weathering, degassing and mixing, so it needs a source and a transport route
rungs.loss_process: nothing destroys it, but the supply can stop
rungs.description: A filter. It changes what is present in a place without any copying, any inheritance or any competition between variants.

rungs.name: thermodynamic partitioning
rungs.mechanism: redox and acid-base reaction, driven by free-energy differences
rungs.loss_process: back reaction to the stable form
rungs.description: A filter. It changes what is present in a place without any copying, any inheritance or any competition between variants.

rungs.name: kinetic persistence
rungs.mechanism: no transport at all, it only has to wait, which needs a kinetic barrier
rungs.description: A filter. It changes what is present in a place without any copying, any inheritance or any competition between variants.

rungs.name: accumulation and concentration
rungs.to_reservoir: a surface, a pore or a film
rungs.mechanism: adsorption, drying, thermophoresis, precipitation, so it needs a flux or a gradient
rungs.description: A filter. A mineral surface that adsorbs one nucleotide and not another is filtering.

rungs.name: autocatalytic amplification
rungs.mechanism: condensation on a surface or in a mineral interlayer, feeding a self-amplifying network
rungs.description: Selection proper, in that it changes relative abundance through differential propagation. A ribozyme that copies itself faster than its neighbour is being selected.

rungs.name: Darwinian selection
rungs.mechanism: template copying, which needs heritable variation
rungs.loss_process: copying error, and loss of the template
rungs.description: Selection proper, in that it changes relative abundance through differential propagation. Levels S4 and S5 are biology and are much harder to time.

rungs.name: Preservation
rungs.to_reservoir: a persistent ecosystem, and then a readable trace in rock
rungs.mechanism: Recycling inside a community, then chemical inertness plus a protective mineral or macromolecular matrix
rungs.loss_process: Community collapse and nutrient exhaustion; then hydrolysis, oxidation, thermal cracking, isotope exchange and recrystallisation during burial and metamorphism
rungs.unit_selected: the refractory subset, which is not the functional subset
rungs.description: S6 comes after S5 and does not consume the pre-LUCA budget. It is a filter on the evidence rather than on life. Nothing about S6 had to happen before LUCA existed. But S6 decides what we are allowed to see, so it decides which of the earlier rungs can ever be tested against a rock. Two gates have to be passed in order. First the lineage has to become a community, because LUCA was not alone and a single cell line in a single vessel leaves no measurable trace. Second, some product of that community has to be chemically inert enough, and physically protected enough, to survive four billion years of burial.

regimes.name: Availability
regimes.expected_legacy: Fe-S and Ni chemistry, tungsten used before molybdenum
regimes.what_is_selected: Selection acts on what is available and soluble. Availability is the filter.

regimes.name: Persistence
regimes.conditions: Cooler, stabilised hydrosphere, still high ultraviolet
regimes.expected_legacy: Photostable subset survives, the phosphate compromise, nitrogen stored or lost
regimes.what_is_selected: Selection acts on survival of molecules. Persistence is the filter.

regimes.name: Throughput
regimes.expected_legacy: Wood-Ljungdahl style CO2 fixation, chemiosmotic coupling
regimes.what_is_selected: Selection acts on whole reaction networks. Throughput is the filter.

regimes.name: Fidelity
regimes.expected_legacy: LUCA as a snapshot of R4, not of R1
regimes.what_is_selected: Selection acts on inherited information. Fidelity is the filter, and this is the only regime that classical Darwinian selection describes.

envelope_events.label: Accretion and magma ocean
envelope_events.note: No liquid water surface. Sets the physical start of the envelope.

envelope_events.label: Moon-forming impact
envelope_events.note: Surface remelted and ocean vaporised. Any earlier chemistry is erased.

envelope_events.label: First evidence of liquid water
envelope_events.note: Single detrital zircon. One grain, so treated as a point, not a range.
envelope_events.source: Hazen et al.; Krissansen-Totton et al.

envelope_events.label: Earliest continuous habitability
envelope_events.note: From about 4.34 Ga. The near end of the envelope is set here, by the planet rather than by biology.
envelope_events.source: Abramov and Mojzsis; Boehnke and Harrison

envelope_events.label: LUCA age estimate
envelope_events.note: Central value 4.2 Ga. This is the far end of the envelope.

envelope_events.label: Jack Hills zircon graphite
envelope_events.note: Contested biosignature. Shown open to mark the dispute.
envelope_events.source: Review of the earliest evidence for life

envelope_events.label: Isua graphite and inclusions
envelope_events.source: Review of the earliest evidence for life

envelope_events.label: Available budget, LUCA at 4.2 Ga
envelope_events.note: About 200 Myr. This is the working budget of the paper.

handoffs.species_and_handoff: Fe(II) to Fe-S cluster or sulfide
handoffs.why_this_value: Clusters self-assemble from Fe(II) and sulfide in seconds to minutes, and sulfides are geologically long-lived. The clearest pass on the plot.

handoffs.species_and_handoff: S(IV) to metal sulfide or thioester
handoffs.why_this_value: Sulfite is a globally accessible sulfur source in shallow water but is capped near 100 micromolar by photolysis.

handoffs.species_and_handoff: HCN to ferrocyanide, cool and Fe-rich
handoffs.why_this_value: Storage reaction. Works best around pH 8 to 9. Converts a fragile species into a kinetically protected one.

handoffs.species_and_handoff: HCN in a hot acidic pool
handoffs.why_this_value: Same handoff time, but hydrolysis is far faster when hot and acidic. This is the same species failing under different conditions, which is the point of the figure.

handoffs.species_and_handoff: NOx(-) to stored N in an Fe(II) ocean
handoffs.why_this_value: Marginal. Steady-state nitrite and nitrate stay below about one micromolar because ultraviolet light and dissolved iron remove them.
Sits on the diagonal. Outcome depends entirely on local conditions, so no general verdict is claimed.

handoffs.species_and_handoff: Free phosphate to an organic ester
handoffs.why_this_value: A clear fail in free solution. Phosphorylation is slow and free phosphate is removed quickly by calcium. This is why phosphorus is the hardest element at S0 and S1.

Fails the diagonal test, and in absolute terms the handoff needs 10^13 to 10^15 s, which is longer than the age of the Earth, so it is effectively never. Catalysis shortens tau_transfer by about twelve orders of magnitude, which is the arrow on the figure.

handoffs.species_and_handoff: CO2 on an Fe or Ni sulfide surface
handoffs.why_this_value: The catalysis arrow on the figure. Adsorption and the first electron transfer take seconds or less once a suitable surface with sulfur vacancies exists. The barrier is the surface, not the reaction.
key_sources: CO2 dissociation on Fe and Ni surfaces

handoffs.species_and_handoff: RNA oligomer, free in warm water
handoffs.why_this_value: Marginal in free solution. Hydrolysis competes directly with any further handoff.

handoffs.species_and_handoff: RNA oligomer, bound to a mineral surface
handoffs.why_this_value: The surface binding arrow. Binding decouples persistence from the hydrolysis rate that applies in free solution, buying up to million year scales.

handoffs.species_and_handoff: Phosphate onto pumice or other volcanic glass
handoffs.why_this_value: Added in this revision. Adsorption is fast and the substrate is long-lived, so it is one of the clearest passes on the plot, and it is a route around the phosphate problem in the row above.

elements.name: hydrogen
elements.why: Maintained continuously by rock and water reaction, so supply is never the problem. The cost is keeping a gradient, not getting the atom.
elements.notes: Gate, the hardest rung: none. What failure looks like: not applicable. Where the material returns to: not applicable. Route through: Continuous supply from rock and water reaction.
elements.s6_why: Tier C, new in this model: Hydrogen isotopes re-equilibrate with pore water and with metamorphic fluids, so no primary biological hydrogen signal survives from the Archean. The element that powers everything leaves the least trace.

elements.name: oxygen
elements.why: Ubiquitous as water and as oxide surfaces. No rung is hard.
elements.notes: Gate, the hardest rung: none. What failure looks like: not applicable. Where the material returns to: not applicable. Route through: Ubiquitous as water and as oxide surfaces.
elements.s6_why: Tier C, new in this model: Oxygen isotopes in silicates and carbonates do survive and are routinely measured, but they record temperature and water composition rather than biology, so the signal is preserved without being diagnostic.

elements.name: carbon
elements.why: Abundant and stored as atmospheric CO2, but activation is the chokepoint. Strictly downstream of Fe and S, because it needs sulfide catalysis.
elements.notes: Gate, the hardest rung: S4 activation into networks. What failure looks like: no reaction without a catalyst. Where the material returns to: atmospheric CO2. Route through: Returns to the CO2 store. Fe, Ni and S sulfide catalysis opens the gate, so carbon is strictly downstream of iron, nickel and sulfur.
elements.s6_why: Tier C, new in this model: The best preserved of all. Graphite and kerogen are chemically inert and their carbon isotope ratios survive to at least 3.7 Ga, through peak metamorphic temperatures of 500 to 600 C at Isua. Carbon is the reason we have any pre-3.5 Ga evidence at all.

elements.name: nitrogen
elements.why: Activation is instantaneous but prohibitively expensive, and the fast product is destroyed by ultraviolet light and dissolved iron. Accumulation is therefore the hard rung.
elements.notes: Gate, the hardest rung: S3 accumulation. What failure looks like: Fe(II) and ultraviolet light destroy fixed N. Where the material returns to: ferrocyanide, alkaline-lake cyanide, vent and crustal ammonium. Route through: Returns to a kinetically protected store, or it is lost outright. The storage step is what buys the time.
elements.s6_why: Tier C, new in this model: Nitrogen isotopes in kerogen are measurable in Archean rocks, but nitrogen is lost preferentially during thermal maturation and the remaining ratio drifts, so the primary value has to be reconstructed rather than read.

elements.name: phosphorus
elements.why: Hard at the very first rungs. Free phosphate is scarce and is removed by calcium. Escape routes are alkaline calcium-poor waters, reduced phosphorus, and adsorption onto volcanic glass.
elements.notes: Gate, the hardest rung: S0 and S1 availability. What failure looks like: calcium phosphate takes it out of solution. Where the material returns to: calcium phosphate, adsorbed on volcanic glass. Route through: Escapes through alkaline carbonate-rich calcium-poor waters, reduced phosphorus, or adsorption onto pumice and other volcanic glass.
elements.s6_why: Tier C, new in this model: Phosphorus survives as apatite, which is highly stable, but demonstrating that a given apatite is biological rather than diagenetic is very difficult, so the element is preserved while its biological attribution is not.

elements.name: sulfur
elements.why: Easy to supply and easy to use, but local accumulation is capped by photolysis of sulfite.
elements.notes: Gate, the hardest rung: S3 accumulation. What failure looks like: photolysis caps sulfite. Where the material returns to: metal sulfide. Route through: Returns to metal sulfide, then concentrates locally where sulfides precipitate.
elements.s6_why: Tier C, new in this model: Sulfide and sulfate sulfur isotopes, and in particular the multiple sulfur isotope signature, survive to 3.5 Ga and beyond and are among the strongest biosignatures we have. Sulfur passes the preservation rung nearly as well as carbon.

elements.name: iron
elements.why: Soluble, abundant and redox-active in an anoxic ocean. No rung is hard, which is why the iron relay completes so easily.
elements.notes: Gate, the hardest rung: none. What failure looks like: not applicable. Where the material returns to: not applicable. Route through: Soluble, abundant and redox-active in an anoxic ocean.
elements.s6_why: Tier C, new in this model: Iron is locked into oxides, sulfides and carbonates that survive indefinitely, and iron isotopes in banded iron formation are readable. Iron passes every rung including this one, which is why the iron relay is the easiest story to tell and the easiest to test.

elements.name: nickel
elements.why: Roughly three orders of magnitude scarcer than iron in seawater, so supply is tight but not blocked. The hard rung is local accumulation, and it is reached by the same sulfide chemistry that concentrates iron, which means nickel and iron pass or fail together. Its legacy is unusually specific: carbon monoxide dehydrogenase and acetyl-CoA synthase, [NiFe] hydrogenase and methyl-coenzyme M reductase all sit close to the root.
elements.notes: Gate, the hardest rung: S3 accumulation. What failure looks like: stays too dilute to reach a working concentration. Where the material returns to: iron-nickel sulfides and alloys. Route through: Concentrates only where iron and nickel sulfides form, so it passes on the same chemistry as iron and pays for the catalyst that opens the carbon gate. Status in this version: Carried, added in this revision. Scarce, so its hard rung is local accumulation rather than supply, but it is the element that pays for the catalyst that opens the carbon gate. Carbon monoxide dehydrogenase and acetyl-CoA synthase, [NiFe] hydrogenase and methyl-coenzyme M reductase are all nickel enzymes and all sit close to the root of the tree.
elements.s6_why: Tier C, new in this model: Nickel is retained in sediments and the nickel to iron ratio of Archean rocks is measurable and has been used to argue about methanogen abundance, but nickel has no isotopic biosignature that is clean enough to stand alone.

elements.name: magnesium
elements.why: Availability was never the problem, since seawater has always been rich in magnesium. The problem is competition. Under strict anoxia Fe(II) is the better cofactor for ribozyme folding and catalysis, so it occupied the divalent cation seat first and magnesium took over only when rising oxygen removed soluble iron. Magnesium does not fail its passage, it is held at S4 by an element that arrived earlier.
elements.notes: Gate, the hardest rung: S4 activation into networks. What failure looks like: no failure of supply; the seat is simply already taken. Where the material returns to: not applicable, it stays dissolved. Route through: Always available, but Fe(II) held the folding and catalytic role first. Magnesium takes over when oxygen strips soluble iron out of the water. Status in this version: Carried, added in this revision. The clearest case of a substitution coupling. Never limiting in seawater, but held out of its modern folding and catalytic role because Fe(II) filled that role first under anoxia. Gives a dated prediction, the second half of prediction 2 in Section 11.2: the switch should track ocean oxygenation and not a lineage split.
elements.s6_why: Tier C, new in this model: There is no preserved biological magnesium signal. Magnesium sits in carbonates and clays that exchange readily, so the substitution story between Fe(II) and Mg(2+) has to be argued from modern biochemistry and from laboratory ribozyme work rather than from rock.

couplings.what_it_does: Fe(II) destroys fixed nitrogen. Iron is both catalyst and executioner: the same abundance that makes the iron relay easy is what removes nitrogen oxides from solution.
Iron, nickel and sulfur catalysts unlock CO2. Carbon activation cannot precede iron and sulfur availability. Lightning interfacial electrochemistry does both jobs in one discharge.

Fe(II) held the divalent cation seat that magnesium holds today. Under strict anoxia an L1 ligase ribozyme is about 25 times more active with Fe(II) than with Mg(II) at 100 micromolar, and a hammerhead ribozyme about 3.5 times more active at 25 micromolar. The handover tracks ocean oxygenation, not a biological innovation.
key_sources: Fe(II) as the early divalent cation

couplings.what_it_does: Phosphate competes with calcium, and with iron, for the same precipitation chemistry. Whichever wins decides whether phosphorus stays in solution.

cycles.name: Wet and dry
cycles.note: Little change in period, but more numerous and shorter-lived pools. One full drying and rewetting event is one polymerisation opportunity and takes hours.

cycles.name: Day and night
cycles.note: About 6 to 17 hours in the Hadean. The fastest predictable cycle available, which is why Gatenby et al. put it at the centre of early information.

cycles.name: Hot and cold, local
cycles.note: Set by local mixing rather than by planetary rotation, so it does not change between today and the Hadean.

cycles.name: Tides
cycles.note: The Moon was much closer, so the period was shorter and the amplitude far larger. Tidal modulation also reaches deep vent flow, which is why dark settings are not excluded from the predictable cycling argument.

cycles.name: pH and redox at interfaces
cycles.note: Continuous rather than periodic, so it is drawn as a band. Range given as low and high rather than a single period.

cycles.name: Raft transit and beaching
cycles.note: Months to about two years per clast. A raft crosses thousands of kilometres in 7 to 8 months and stays afloat about 20 months, delivering a sequence of settings to the same parcel of material.

scenarios.name: Alkaline hydrothermal vent
scenarios.reasoning: The setting exists as soon as there is an ocean and recurs constantly, so T1 is tiny. The total is essentially the 1 to 10 Myr of Class 3 plus a coincidence term. Comfortable fit.
scenarios.site_note: Tier C, derived for this model: not a workbook value and new to the model. Order of magnitude count of independent parallel vessels or attempts, read off the reasoning text for this row and the T3 definition on the Method_time_budgets sheet, where T3 is the number of independent attempts needed divided by the rate at which independent attempts are generated. Here a vent field is of order 10^3 to 10^6 independent mixing interfaces, since the sheet says these settings come in enormous numbers and recur constantly, and each chimney holds many separate pores a few micrometres apart.

scenarios.name: Subaerial wet and dry pools
scenarios.reasoning: Requires land above sea level in the Hadean, which is contested. The fit therefore depends on a geological question, not a chemical one. Fits, but with little room to spare.
scenarios.site_note: Tier C, derived for this model: not a workbook value and new to the model. Order of magnitude count of independent parallel vessels or attempts, read off the reasoning text for this row and the T3 definition on the Method_time_budgets sheet, where T3 is the number of independent attempts needed divided by the rate at which independent attempts are generated. Here a subaerial pond is of order 1 to 10^3 vessels, since the Method_time_budgets sheet says a pond is one vessel and the amount of Hadean land above sea level is contested, so only a small number of pool fields can be assumed.

scenarios.name: Impact-generated hydrothermal system
scenarios.reasoning: Impacts were frequent and each system runs for of order 10^5 years, so both T1 and T3 are small. The fastest of the classical settings.
scenarios.site_note: Tier C, derived for this model: not a workbook value and new to the model. Order of magnitude count of independent parallel vessels or attempts, read off the reasoning text for this row and the T3 definition on the Method_time_budgets sheet, where T3 is the number of independent attempts needed divided by the rate at which independent attempts are generated. Here of order 10^2 to 10^5 sites, taken from the sheet's statement that impacts were frequent and each system runs for of order 10^5 years, so several hydrothermal fields with many pores each are live at any time.

scenarios.name: Pumice raft and tidal beaching
scenarios.reasoning: T3 collapses because an eruption supplies of order 10^12 independent clasts rather than one pond, and the sequence of settings is delivered to the material. The required duration is set by how often suitable eruptions happened.
scenarios.site_note: Tier C, derived for this model: not a workbook value and new to the model. Order of magnitude count of independent parallel vessels or attempts, read off the reasoning text for this row and the T3 definition on the Method_time_budgets sheet, where T3 is the number of independent attempts needed divided by the rate at which independent attempts are generated. Here of order 10^12 clasts per eruption, which the Fig8 and Method_time_budgets sheets state explicitly, and which is why T3 collapses for this family.

scenarios.name: Icy or eutectic concentration
scenarios.reasoning: Sustained freezing is hard to arrange on a hot young planet, and low temperature slows every rate constant, so the chemistry itself starts to cost real time. Needs the longer budget.
scenarios.site_note: Tier C, derived for this model: not a workbook value and new to the model. Order of magnitude count of independent parallel vessels or attempts, read off the reasoning text for this row and the T3 definition on the Method_time_budgets sheet, where T3 is the number of independent attempts needed divided by the rate at which independent attempts are generated. Here of order 1 to 10^3 brine pockets, a pond-like count, because sustained freezing is hard to arrange on a hot young planet so only a few such settings exist at once.

scenarios.name: Panspermia-assisted delivery
scenarios.reasoning: Pays a full origin sequence on a host body, then adds host habitability onset, an ejecting impact, transit, and arrival and establishment. Only a small fraction of ejecta arrives viable, so many delivery attempts are needed and T3 rises steeply. Strictly larger than the best terrestrial case.
scenarios.site_note: Tier C, derived for this model: not a workbook value and new to the model. Order of magnitude count of independent parallel vessels or attempts, read off the reasoning text for this row and the T3 definition on the Method_time_budgets sheet, where T3 is the number of independent attempts needed divided by the rate at which independent attempts are generated. Here of order 1 to 10^2 delivery attempts that matter, because only a small fraction of ejecta arrives viable, so the effective number of independent parallel sites at the receiving end is small even though the ejecta count is large.

terms.name: Setting availability and recurrence
terms.what_it_measures: How long you must wait for the physical setting to exist, and how often it comes back if a single instance is destroyed.
terms.how_estimated: Vents and impact-driven systems are available essentially as soon as there is an ocean, so T1 is small. Subaerial pools need land above sea level, which is genuinely contested for the Hadean, so T1 is large. Cold eutectic settings need sustained freezing on a planet with a hot interior and a faint young Sun, so T1 is large.

terms.name: Chemistry, Class 1 and Class 2 steps
terms.what_it_measures: The actual reaction and transport time, once the setting exists.
terms.how_estimated: Class 1 steps run in microseconds to hours and Class 2 steps in days to thousands of years. Even a Class 2 step of 1000 years is 0.001 Myr, so T2 is negligible in every terrestrial scenario. This is the main result of Section 10: the chemistry is not what consumes the budget.

terms.name: Coincidence waiting time
terms.what_it_measures: How long you must wait for several fast steps to occur in the same place, in the right order, before a flood, impact or dilution event resets the attempt. Read it as (number of independent attempts needed) divided by (rate at which independent attempts are generated).
terms.how_estimated: This is the term that actually consumes a short budget. It falls when the number of independent vessels rises. A pond is one vessel. A pumice eruption supplies of order 10^12 clasts, which is why the raft scenario sits at the fast end even though each individual clast only stays afloat for about 20 months.

terms.name: Slow biological steps, Class 3
terms.what_it_measures: Crossing the error threshold and establishing heritability, then fixing a trait or enzyme family in a population.
terms.how_estimated: Standard estimates for fixation are 10^6 to 10^7 years, so 1 to 10 Myr. Every scenario pays this, so it sets the floor of about 1 Myr on the whole figure. No scenario can be faster than its slowest Class 3 step.

audit_method.budget_note: The available budget is arithmetic. 200 Myr is the interval from the end of the Moon-forming impact aftermath at about 4.40 Ga to a LUCA at 4.2 Ga: start 4.40 Ga, which is the first evidence of liquid water and the end of the Moon-forming impact aftermath at 4.36 Ga, end 4.2 Ga, the central LUCA estimate, so 4.40 minus 4.20 = 0.20 Gyr, about 200 Myr. 600 Myr is the same interval taken to a LUCA at 3.8 Ga: 4.40 minus 3.80 = 0.60 Gyr, about 600 Myr. Figure 8 shows both lines so the reader can see which scenarios depend on which date. The required duration is a sum of four terms, three of which are judgements, and the sum is then rounded to the nearest order of magnitude for the figure, which is why the plotted range and the component sum differ slightly.
audit_method.trials_note: Number of trials in a budget is the budget in seconds divided by the period of the driving cycle. A 100 Myr budget is 3.156 x 10^15 s. Divided by a 20 hour Hadean day (7.2 x 10^4 s) that is about 4.4 x 10^10 diurnal cycles. Tides at about 7 x 10^3 s give roughly an order of magnitude more. This is the number that matters for driven chemistry, where the cycle powers the reaction, rather than the ratio Pi. A 200 Myr budget is 6.311 x 10^15 s.
audit_method.caveat: One caveat that is stated in the manuscript and is worth repeating here: Figure 8 audits duration only. Passing the duration test is necessary but not sufficient. A scenario can fit the budget comfortably and still fail on other grounds, for example on whether it supplies a fast predictable cycle at all.

free_energy.note: Live check of the concentration cost, computed rather than asserted, with R = 8.314 J per mole per kelvin, T = 298.15 K and a concentration factor of 1000. It returns 17.1 kJ per mole, which is the same value as three pH units across a membrane, because three pH units is a proton activity ratio of one thousand. The equality is arithmetic, not a coincidence, and it is why a pH gradient and a concentration gradient are the same currency.

pi_examples.pair: Iron-rich anoxic oceans against enzyme family fixation
pi_examples.reading: Pi is far above one, so composition is locked in and conserved. Iron-sulfur clusters are everywhere, still.

pi_examples.pair: Iron-rich anoxic oceans against slower fixation
pi_examples.reading: Same pair at the slow end of the fixation estimate. Pi is still about 100, so the conclusion does not depend on which end you take.

pi_examples.pair: Archean metal availability shifts against metabolic innovation
pi_examples.reading: Pi is about one, so expect recruitment, turnover and replacement rather than conservation, and regulation rather than fixed composition.

pi_examples.pair: Diurnal ultraviolet cycling against lineage-level fixation
pi_examples.reading: Pi is about 2 x 10^-9. No imprint of any particular day survives, but there is strong general selection for photoprotection and repair. Because the day is also predictable, expect anticipation as well as buffering. Section 7.2 of the manuscript now quotes about 2 x 10^-9 for this row, from a 20 hour day of 2.3 x 10^-3 years divided by a fixation time of 10^6 years, so the text and this row now agree.

measurement_gaps.gap: Rung affected: S3 to S4. What is already known: Amino acid intercalation into Mg-Al layered double hydroxide is demonstrated by the reconstruction method at 0.9 to 2.7 mmol per gram for every amino acid tested except lysine and arginine, where ion exchange failed. Reactive end to end alignment during drying is modelled, with up to 25 per cent of alanines in reactive arrangements, a maximum at about 2 water molecules per amino acid, and a layer thickness of 0.53 nm. Alanine dipeptide formation on brucite-like layers under wet and dry cycling is measured. Nobody has run it in green rust, which has a redox-active layer with Fe(II) as the divalent cation.
measurement_gaps.why_it_matters: Which audit term it moves: Coincidence waiting time, term 3
measurement_gaps.what_would_settle_it: Oligomer length distribution and yield per wet and dry cycle in green rust with carbonate and with sulfate interlayers, under strict anoxia.
measurement_gaps.linked_prediction: Tier C, derived for this model: prediction 5, rates and the cycle budget, because the gap sets the yield per wet and dry cycle.

measurement_gaps.gap: Rung affected: S1 to S2. What is already known: Structural Fe(II) in green rust reduces nitrite to ammonium with a pseudo-first-order constant of about 4.1 x 10^-5 per second, a half life of about 4.7 hours, while dissolved Fe(II) reduces nitrite to N2O gas. The published second-order constants for the dissolved route are inconsistent between the source table and its running text.
measurement_gaps.why_it_matters: Which audit term it moves: Whether nitrogen passes at all, term 2 and term 3
measurement_gaps.what_would_settle_it: The branch ratio between N2O loss and ammonium retention as a function of iron speciation, pH and salt content, reported in one consistent set of units.
measurement_gaps.linked_prediction: Tier C, derived for this model: prediction 1, the iron against nitrogen coupling, because the gap decides whether fixed nitrogen is retained or destroyed.

measurement_gaps.gap: Rung affected: S3 to S4. What is already known: Simple iron sulfur clusters assemble spontaneously from Fe(II) and sulfide in seconds to minutes, and the ferredoxin fold is the most conserved fold in the tree of life. What is not measured is the competition between capture by a short peptide and loss by oxidation or aggregation.
measurement_gaps.why_it_matters: Which audit term it moves: Coincidence waiting time, term 3
measurement_gaps.what_would_settle_it: The rate of [Fe4S4] capture by a short ferredoxin-like peptide against the oxidation and aggregation rate, at prebiotic iron and sulfide concentrations.
measurement_gaps.linked_prediction: Tier C, derived for this model: prediction 4, the handoff line, because the gap is a direct race between capture and loss.

measurement_gaps.gap: Rung affected: S4. What is already known: Acetyl phosphate forms from thioacetate and phosphate at about 2 per cent yield in 1 to 2 hours at 20 mM phosphate. Magnesium roughly doubles the yield, no acetyl phosphate forms at pH 11, and Fe2+ has little effect. Prebiotic ocean phosphate was micromolar, not millimolar.
measurement_gaps.why_it_matters: Which audit term it moves: Class 2 chemistry, term 2
measurement_gaps.what_would_settle_it: Acetyl phosphate yield at micromolar phosphate rather than 20 mM, with and without a concentrating surface.
measurement_gaps.linked_prediction: Tier C, derived for this model: prediction 5, rates and the cycle budget, because the gap is a Class 2 yield at prebiotic phosphate concentrations.

measurement_gaps.gap: Rung affected: S4 to S5. What is already known: Wet and dry cycling drives condensation, and the same cycling hydrolyses what it makes. Bulk yields of long oligonucleotides from non-activated nucleotides are at or below about one per cent per cycle.
measurement_gaps.why_it_matters: Which audit term it moves: Cycle count and the S4 to S5 chokepoint, term 3 and term 4
measurement_gaps.what_would_settle_it: Template strand-length half life measured under exactly the wet and dry cycle that drives the condensation, rather than under steady conditions.
measurement_gaps.linked_prediction: Tier C, derived for this model: prediction 5, rates and the cycle budget, since it is the low yield of long polymers from wet and dry cycling where the manuscript says the pressure currently sits.

measurement_gaps.gap: Rung affected: S4 to S5. What is already known: Modern folding and catalysis at the ribosome depend on Mg2+, but an anoxic Hadean ocean would have offered Fe(II) at comparable or higher activity. The crossover has not been measured for a folding site.
measurement_gaps.why_it_matters: Which audit term it moves: Prediction 2 and the composition axis
measurement_gaps.what_would_settle_it: The Fe(II) to Mg activity ratio at which a folding site switches its preferred cation, under strict anoxia.
measurement_gaps.linked_prediction: Prediction 2 and the composition axis, as stated on the Measurement_gaps sheet.

predictions.title: Coupling: iron against nitrogen
predictions.expectation: Because Fe(II) destroys fixed nitrogen, the deepest nitrogen machinery should be import-based, not fixation-based.

predictions.title: Ordering of metals
predictions.expectation: Metal use in the most conserved enzyme families should follow the order in which those metals became available. Two cases are sharp enough to test on their own: tungsten is soluble in reduced water while molybdenum is not, so the oldest members of the relevant families should be tungsten-using (Schoepp-Cothenet et al.); and if Fe(II) was the early divalent cation, the switch to magnesium should track ocean oxygenation rather than any biological innovation.
predictions.broken_by: a conserved dependence on a metal that became bioavailable only after LUCA, a phylogeny placing molybdenum ancestral to tungsten, or a magnesium switch well before oxygen rose. The tungsten case is a live risk rather than a safe bet, because isotope work already traces use of both metals to at least 3.4 Ga.

predictions.title: Gating of carbon
predictions.expectation: Carbon fixation should always sit downstream of transition metal and sulfide chemistry.
predictions.broken_by: evidence for ancestral carbon fixation without metal sulfide catalysis.

predictions.title: The handoff line, and photostability as its clearest case
predictions.expectation: Species that plot below the diagonal should be absent from conserved biochemistry unless they had a storage route, and the sharpest version of that claim is about light: retained bases, chromophores and side chains should be more photostable than the prebiotic alternatives that were not retained.
predictions.broken_by: a retained species with no plausible store, or a systematic survey showing no photostability enrichment.

predictions.title: Rates and the cycle budget
predictions.expectation: Steps we call Class 1 or Class 2 should be reproducible in the laboratory inside the stated timescales, and no required process may need more cycles than the budget allows, which is 10^10 to 10^11 for a diurnal process.
predictions.broken_by: a step we call fast that resists completion over years of cycling, or a required process shown to need more cycles than are available. The low yields of long polymers from wet and dry cycling (Eiby 2025) are where this pressure currently sits.

predictions.title: Substrate test for glass
predictions.expectation: Normalised per square metre of glass surface rather than per gram, silicic pumice should be a weaker polymerisation catalyst than mafic glass such as diabase (Jerome et al. 2022).
predictions.broken_by: pumice matching or beating mafic glass once surface area is controlled for, which would strengthen the pumice case rather than the framework. Either result is informative.

predictions.title: Composition of the oldest carbonaceous inclusions
predictions.expectation: The framework says nitrogen passed by storage, that phosphorus was scarce in water but concentrated on surfaces, and that both were present in a working cell well before the oldest rocks we can read. Isua-type carbonaceous inclusions armoured in metamorphic minerals should therefore carry carbon bonded to nitrogen and to phosphate, which is what has been reported (Hassenkam et al. 2017).
predictions.broken_by: a larger, better-controlled survey of comparable inclusions showing nitrogen and phosphate systematically absent where carbon is present and demonstrably biogenic.

predictions.title: The budget falsifier
predictions.expectation: A well-supported revision of LUCA to 3.9 Ga or younger relaxes the budget and re-admits the slow, land-dependent scenarios. We state in advance how we would update: the ladder, the handoff criterion and the couplings are unaffected, because they are about rates and not dates, but the audit in Figure 8 changes and the conclusion of Section 10 becomes weaker rather than wrong.
predictions.broken_by: This prediction is itself the falsifier for the audit: a well-supported LUCA date of 3.9 Ga or younger would relax the budget and re-admit the scenarios that Figure 8 currently excludes.

gates.name: Ecosystem persistence
gates.criterion: Da_eco = vessel lifetime divided by nutrient recycling time. This is the same handoff criterion applied to a community instead of a molecule.
gates.reading: One turnover is a population that lives once and dies. Many turnovers is an ecosystem that recycles, cross-feeds and keeps going after any single cell dies. The reconstructed gene set of LUCA is that of a chemolithoautotroph living on hydrogen, carbon dioxide, nitrogen and transition metals, and it already carries dependencies that only make sense if other organisms were supplying things, so the community, not the cell, is the unit that survived.

parameters.label: Vessel lifetime
parameters.note: An impact-generated hydrothermal system runs for of order 10^5 years. A single pond may last years. A vent field can last far longer.

parameters.label: Nutrient recycling time
parameters.note: How long it takes the community to turn its limiting nutrient over once. Modern microbial mats do this in days to years.

parameters.label: Turnovers needed to call it an ecosystem
parameters.note: New to this model. There is no measured value. It is the number of recycling cycles needed before functional differentiation and cross-feeding can be established.

sources.citation: Weiss et al. 2016, The physiology and habitat of the last universal common ancestor

gates.name: Rock-record preservation
gates.criterion: tau_degradation at the burial temperature must exceed the age of the rock, and the rock must not have passed the thermal maturity ceiling.
gates.reading: Two separate things can destroy a molecular trace. One is slow chemistry over a very long time, which the Arrhenius calculation covers. The other is a short hot event, which no amount of time-averaging survives. Above roughly 150 degrees C the oil window closes and only methane is left. Above greenschist metamorphism carbon atoms exchange with their surroundings, so even the carbon isotope value starts to drift.
gates.tier: Tier A for the half-lives, Tier B for the extrapolation

parameters.label: Burial temperature
parameters.note: Average temperature the material sat at, not the peak. For Isua the peak was 500 to 600 C.

parameters.label: Age of the rock
parameters.note: Isua is 3.7 to 3.8 Ga. Jack Hills zircons reach 4.4 Ga.

parameters.label: Activation energy for degradation
parameters.note: Derived in the app from measured RNA phosphodiester hydrolysis at two temperatures. Higher values make extrapolation to low temperature much more optimistic, which is exactly why this parameter should be tweaked and watched.

molecule_classes.name: RNA, phosphodiester backbone
molecule_classes.bond_types: phosphodiester, plus a 2 prime hydroxyl that attacks its own backbone
molecule_classes.why: The 2 prime hydroxyl group next to the phosphodiester linkage attacks the backbone from the inside. The molecule is built to be cleaved. Nothing in the geological record can hold it.

molecule_classes.name: Free nucleobases, adenine and guanine
molecule_classes.bond_types: glycosidic and ring carbon nitrogen bonds
molecule_classes.second_point: about 1 yr at 100 C, and 6 x 10^5 to 1.3 x 10^6 yr at 0 C
molecule_classes.why: Even at freezing point the most stable bases reach only about a million years. That is three to four orders of magnitude short of the Archean. Cytosine is far worse at 340 years at 25 C, which is a separate and well known problem for any RNA-first account.

molecule_classes.name: Peptides and proteins
molecule_classes.second_point: oldest recovered sequences reach 3.8 Myr chronological age, and only when bound inside a mineral
molecule_classes.why: Amide bonds hydrolyse and amino acids racemise. The record stops in the millions of years even with mineral binding, which is about a thousand times short of the Archean. Mineral binding does buy real time, which is the same effect the model uses for RNA on a surface, but it is not enough.

molecule_classes.name: Sugars and free phosphate esters
molecule_classes.second_point: ribose degrades on timescales of hours to weeks at moderate temperature and neutral pH
molecule_classes.why: These are the most reactive functional molecules in the whole sequence, which is exactly why they work as chemistry and exactly why they leave nothing.

molecule_classes.name: Hopanes and steranes, saturated hydrocarbon skeletons
molecule_classes.role_in_life: membrane rigidity, from hopanols and sterols
molecule_classes.bond_types: carbon carbon and carbon hydrogen only, no hydrolysable bond
molecule_classes.second_point: stable for billions of years in rocks that stayed below the end of the oil window, but absent from every Archean sequence tested so far
molecule_classes.polarity: non polar, essentially insoluble in water
molecule_classes.verdict: preserved, but not in any Archean rock yet found
molecule_classes.why: There is no bond for water to attack and the molecule will not dissolve. Diagenesis strips the one alcohol group off the precursor, so the fossil is chemically more inert than the living molecule was. The limit is not time, it is heat: ultraclean Archean drill cores put total hopanes below 37.9 picograms per gram and total steranes below 32.9 picograms per gram, indistinguishable from the blanks, and the authors conclude that no currently known Archean strata lie within the thermal maturity window in which these molecules could have survived.

molecule_classes.name: Kerogen, cross-linked macromolecular residue
molecule_classes.role_in_life: not a biomolecule, it is what is left of many
molecule_classes.bond_types: aromatic and aliphatic carbon network, insoluble and non hydrolysable
molecule_classes.second_point: survives to at least 3.7 Ga and retains a carbon isotope signal
molecule_classes.polarity: insoluble in water and in organic solvents
molecule_classes.why: Kerogen forms in two ways that both favour inertness. Resistant, non hydrolysable biomacromolecules are selectively preserved while everything hydrolysable is destroyed, and degradation products repolymerise into a random insoluble network. The result traps whatever is inside it and has almost nothing left for water to react with.

molecule_classes.name: Graphitic carbon and carbon isotope ratios
molecule_classes.role_in_life: none, it is the end product
molecule_classes.second_point: the Isua rocks reached peak metamorphic temperatures of 500 to 600 C and the graphite still carries a preserved carbon isotope composition
molecule_classes.verdict: preserved, and the only molecular class that reaches 3.7 Ga
molecule_classes.why: Nothing is left to destroy except the isotope ratio itself, and that only starts to drift above greenschist metamorphism, where carbon atoms begin exchanging with their surroundings. This is why the earliest evidence for life is an isotope ratio and a texture rather than a molecule.

molecule_classes.name: Mineral-hosted organic inclusions
molecule_classes.bond_types: mixed, but shielded by the host crystal
molecule_classes.polarity: not applicable, the host controls access
molecule_classes.verdict: preserved by the matrix rather than by the molecule
molecule_classes.why: A crystal that closes around the material removes water and oxidant access, so the protection is physical instead of chemical. This is the same trick as RNA bound to a mineral surface in the handoff table, taken to its limit, and it is why inclusion studies are the most promising route to pre-3.5 Ga organic evidence.

why_refractory.point: Function requires reactive bonds, and reactive bonds are the ones water attacks
why_refractory.detail: Every molecule that does chemical work in a cell does it through a hydrolysable bond: the phosphoester in RNA and ATP, the amide in a peptide, the thioester in acetyl coenzyme A, the hemiacetal in a sugar. The reactivity is the function. So the molecules that carry out S4 activation and S5 heritable use are, by construction, the least preservable molecules in the whole sequence. This is not bad luck. It is the same property seen from two directions.

why_refractory.point: The molecules that survive were built for insulation, not for chemistry
why_refractory.detail: Lipid skeletons exist to keep water out of a membrane interior. To do that they are made of carbon and hydrogen only, with no polar group and no hydrolysable bond. That makes them useless as catalysts and almost indestructible as fossils. Preservation therefore samples the structural side of biochemistry and misses the functional side entirely.

why_refractory.point: Diagenesis makes the survivors more inert than they were alive
why_refractory.detail: A sterol becomes a sterane and a hopanol becomes a hopane by losing its single alcohol group and having its double bonds saturated. The fossil molecule is a stripped down version of the biological one. Preservation is not passive storage, it is a further filter that removes whatever reactivity was left.

why_refractory.point: A matrix can protect a molecule that could not protect itself
why_refractory.detail: Cross-linking into kerogen, or enclosure inside a growing crystal, removes water and oxidant access. This is physical protection rather than chemical inertness, and it is the only route by which anything polar reaches the deep record at all. It is the geological version of the surface binding arrow in the handoff figure.

Before S5 there were no lipid membranes producing long hydrocarbon skeletons and no macromolecular network to trap anything. The inventory was small, polar, hydrolysable species at micromolar concentrations. So the absence of pre-LUCA molecular evidence is exactly what the chemistry predicts, and it carries no information about whether that chemistry happened. This is worth stating plainly because the absence is often read as if it were evidence.

The rock record can only ever sample the subset of molecules that pass S6, and that subset is close to disjoint from the molecules that pass S4 and S5. So the earliest evidence for LUCA will be isotopic, textural and inclusion-based rather than molecular, no matter how good the instruments get. Reading the record any other way is reading the preservation filter and mistaking it for history.
